Maladaptive Strategies.value: I work hard at keeping busy with other things
I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't stop bad things from happening to me
I should have protected others and I failed
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.explanation: Fire/flame cues are hard to reconcile with a childhood domestic-violence witnessing trauma profile when the rest of the trigger, memory, threat, and appraisal items do not suggest fire, arson, or burn-related trauma content. This trigger appears trauma-incongruent rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
issues.explanation: 'No longer capable of doing the things that defined me' suggests a loss of prior adult identity/functioning that is difficult to fit with a 19-year-old whose index trauma was childhood witnessed domestic violence. The other appraisals center on helplessness and failed protection, which fit better; this item is comparatively implausible for the developmental context.

vignette: Ana María, a 19-year-old train conductor, first noticed the phantom echoes of that night when she was nine. The house she lived in had been a battleground of shouts, broken glass, and a husband who turned a wife into a silent witness. The memory of a man's heavy boots slamming against the floor still tasted like iron and fear. Even now, in the dark corridors of the rail yards and the dimly lit platforms she patrols, the triggers she carries-darkness that swallows the light, a sudden thud that makes her heart pound, and the screech of a train horn-unfold a flood of the past. Each of those sensory sparks pulls her back into the event, as if the house had never closed, and the past is still unsealed. The darkness on the tracks does more than remind her of the night the windows were shattered. In the blackness of tunnels, the echo of her own racing pulse seems louder than any whistle, and she feels an urgent need to understand why this terror remains alive. That same fear fuels her belief that she is helpless, that she could have stopped it, that she failed to protect someone. The guilt that latches to her mind makes the remembered scene feel all the more present and painful. The weight of those negative appraisals anchors the image in her mind; each time she thinks "I should have done something," the memory surges back, sharper and more vivid. Her terror grows, and she starts to believe that the danger is real and looming again, so she checks the locks on every door and window she can reach, even after the train has arrived and the platform lights are on. The loop tightens as her attempts to regain control create new patterns. To keep from feeling the dread, Ana María fills her schedule with meticulous tasks: she double-checks signal systems, ensures all couplings are secure, and rehearses the emergency drill in her head as if she were in a battlefield. Her busyness, meant to stave off the feeling of vulnerability, ends up sharpening the sense that she must stay vigilant. It also reminds her of the night's helplessness, reinforcing the belief that if she had not taken such actions, the house-and now the train-would have fallen into danger. This cycle of busyness further triggers the memory, as each check echoes a memory of frantic footsteps in a dim hallway, and the taste of iron clings to her tongue whenever a new alarm sounds. Even as she keeps her mind occupied, her heart continues to race in the quiet moments, a reminder that the threat is still alive. The sound of a distant freight train or a sudden clack of metal on steel sends her heart racing again, making her feel as though she is in the middle of a storm she cannot outrun. Each time that threat sounds, she automatically thinks she is still at risk, which pulls her back to the traumatic image. The memory, in turn, amplifies her sense of danger and drives her to stay busy, creating a tightening spiral that feels impossible to escape. She also avoids meals, thinking that if she eats, her mind might relax and let the memory surface again. This undereating, meant to keep her energy sharp, reminds her of the cold, hungry nights she survived by staying awake, feeding her belief that she cannot be safe if she slows down. Ana María's fear has seeped into her personal life, making her avoid evenings outside because the darkness feels like the old living room walls, and she stays alert when loud noises-like the rumble of an approaching freight train-pierce the quiet. She is certain that any lapse could bring the past catastrophe back to life. She has started to doubt whether she can ever feel truly secure on a night shift, and her self-blame grows with each missed train whistle or delayed departure. Her sense that she was the one who failed to stop something bad from happening keeps her trapped in a loop of anxiety that refuses to dissipate. She tells herself that she must always be ready, always be watching, because if she were not, she would be the one who would be hurt. The day she finally asked for help was when the weight of her own thoughts became unbearable. While waiting for the midnight express to arrive, she felt her heart pound so hard it seemed to echo in her chest, and the memory of the house's broken walls returned with a vivid taste of iron. In that instant she realized that staying busy, checking every door, and refusing to eat had not given her peace, but only made her life more exhausting and less safe. She could no longer ignore that the triggers she faced in her job-dark tunnels, sudden noises, her own racing pulse-were not just memories but ongoing threats that made her believe the past could still strike. She wanted relief from the endless cycle of guilt and fear, and most of all, she hoped to find a way to feel safe again on the tracks that once mirrored the darkness of her childhood home.
